August 24, 1908. A single masked man stopped stagecoach after stagecoach near Kepler Cascades. By the most-cited count he robbed seventeen of them and was never caught.

Superintendent Norris claimed Native people were afraid of the geysers. The Park Service says the evidence shows the opposite: tribes had known this land for thousands of years.

May 7, 1894. A new law banned hunting in Yellowstone. It came too late to punish Howell, but it was written because of him. By 1902 only 23 wild bison were left.

George Cowan was shot through the thigh, then in the head, and left for dead. He wasn't dead. He dragged himself about twelve miles through the forest until scouts found him on August 29.

The whole Nez Perce caravan crossed the Yellowstone River near Mud Volcano, hundreds of people and nearly two thousand horses. Today the place is called Nez Perce Ford.

General Howard followed with about 600 men and never caught up. The Nez Perce drew Sturgis away with a feint, then slipped out through a narrow gorge to the Clarks Fork River. They had spent thirteen days in Yellowstone.

In the Bears Paw Mountains, about forty miles from Canada, Army forces under Colonel Nelson Miles attacked. The siege lasted five days in freezing cold, and on October 5, 1877, Joseph handed over his rifle.

On September 14, 2015, a storm over Zion National Park sent a flash flood through Keyhole Canyon. Seven canyoneers were inside. None came out.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#Zion #FlashFlood #NationalParks #Shorts

The Virgin River drops about 71 feet per mile through Zion, and the bare sandstone can't soak up a storm. Every side canyon becomes a funnel. The floods are how the canyon was made.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#Zion #Geology #NationalParks #Shorts

We hiked the Zion Narrows top to bottom in November 2021. Walls a thousand feet high, in places only 20 to 30 feet apart. When the water rises in here, there's often nowhere to climb.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#ZionNarrows #Hiking #NationalParks #Shorts

July 1993: three leaders and five teenage boys tried to descend Kolob Creek in Zion with the water far too high. Two leaders drowned. The last adult and the boys waited four nights on a ledge until rescuers winched them out. All six survived.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#Zion #Rescue #NationalParks #Shorts

On July 4, 2020, a dog died about an hour after playing in the Virgin River. Park scientists found cyanobacteria in the algae making a nerve toxin far above safe levels. Never let your dog drink from the river.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#Zion #DogSafety #NationalParks #Shorts

At least seventeen people have died at Angels Landing in Zion. The last half mile follows a spine of rock with sheer drops on both sides. We climbed it in 2021. Many of the falls didn't happen on the chains at all.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#AngelsLanding #Zion #Hiking #Shorts

Since 2022 you need a lottery permit to climb Angels Landing. Nearly 400,000 were issued in two years, and on the busiest days the odds of winning were as low as 8 percent.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#AngelsLanding #Zion #NationalParks #Shorts

In 2021 park crews hauled almost five tons of human waste off the toilets at Scout Lookout, just below the Angels Landing chains. That's what five million visitors look like.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#Zion #AngelsLanding #NationalParks #Shorts

In 1920 fewer than 4,000 people visited Zion. In 2021 more than five million did, a record. The water and the rock that make Zion beautiful never stop moving.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 1

#Zion #History #NationalParks #Shorts

Hundreds of feet of water once stood where this hotel is. Where Zion Lodge sits today, the lake was about three hundred and fifty to three hundred and eighty feet deep. A mountainside fell, dammed the river, and the lake slowly filled with mud.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #ZionLodge #History #NationalParks

About a minute. That's how long it took a mountainside to fall into Zion Canyon, about four thousand eight hundred years ago. Models suggest the rock averaged about a hundred and twelve miles per hour and peaked near two hundred. The main mass crossed the canyon in about twenty seconds. One geologist who studied it called it a minute with up to ten thousand years of consequences.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #Landslide #Geology #NationalParks

Ninety Hoover Dams. That's how much concrete you'd need to rebuild the mountainside that collapsed into Zion Canyon. About ten billion cubic feet of rock, roughly five times bigger than any landslide in North America's recorded history, not counting volcanoes.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #HooverDam #Landslide #NationalParks

About four hundred and thirty people cut off, and one road gone. On the night of April twelfth, nineteen ninety-five, part of an ancient landslide in Zion moved again. It blocked the Virgin River, and the river cut a new path straight through the road. About six hundred feet of it was destroyed. Guests and employees at Zion Lodge were stuck. Crews carved an emergency detour out of the canyon wall in about twenty-two hours.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #Landslide #History #NationalParks

Two hundred and sixty-five thousand board feet of lumber, down a wire. That's how Zion Lodge was built in nineteen twenty-five. A tramway on Cable Mountain lowered the wood more than two thousand vertical feet to the canyon floor.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #ZionLodge #History #NationalParks

Three thousand feet up, a slab of sandstone let go. August twenty-fourth, twenty nineteen: rock broke off Cable Mountain, above Weeping Rock. More than four hundred and thirty-five thousand cubic feet of debris came down. Three visitors were hurt. Part of a trail was buried under what geologists called a small rock avalanche. The twist? Nearly a century earlier, that same mountain had lowered the lumber for Zion Lodge on a wire.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #Rockfall #CableMountain #NationalParks

A hundred and eight days. On January twenty-sixth, nineteen sixty-six, the main building of Zion Lodge burned. A prefabricated replacement was up and operating a hundred and eight days later. And all of it stands on the bed of an ancient lake.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #ZionLodge #History #NationalParks

Fewer than eighty deer became six hundred. Two Oregon State ecologists argue that when crowds pushed the cougars out of Zion Canyon in the nineteen thirties, the deer boomed. Between nineteen thirty-eight and nineteen forty-seven, the Park Service killed or removed seven hundred and eighty of them. And the deer ate the young cottonwoods. In nearby North Creek, where cougars stayed, the researchers found almost forty times more young trees. It's a debated idea.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #Wildlife #Ecology #NationalParks

Five thousand tons of rock, and no visitor killed. In nineteen sixty-eight, a rockfall that size hit the end of the trail to the Narrows. In Zion, rocks fall often. Yet according to the Park Service, no visitor has ever died from one here.

▶ Full documentary on YouTube: search AlphaDog Studio, Zion Part 2

#Zion #Rockfall #History #NationalParks

A lake that lasted seven hundred years, then filled itself in. When a mountainside fell into Zion Canyon, it dammed the Virgin River, and a lake some call Lake Zion filled the valley. Then the river slowly buried it, dropping sand and mud into the still water, until about four thousand one hundred years ago the lake was full. Not of water. Of sediment. That's the flat floor of Zion Canyon today.
